lesson.grammar_point: probability and trend language (likely to, expected to, rise by)

listenings.text: I have run a weekly forecast for fifteen years, and the number is almost never the problem. The problem is that people give one number when the CEO needs two. The first is the commit: the deals you are almost certain to close, the ones you would bet your bonus on. The second is the best case: everything that could close if the right things happen. When a salesperson gives me a single number, I do not know which of the two it is, and usually neither do they. The other thing I listen for is the direction. A number that is on track but falling every week is more worrying than a number that is short but rising. So in my meetings the rule is simple. Say the number, say how sure you are, say which way it is moving, and name the one deal that is likely to change it. Forty seconds. Anything longer is a story, and stories are how forecasts slip.

Every Monday I get the forecast from six regions, and I can tell in about ten seconds which heads of sales I can trust. It is not the ones with the biggest numbers. It is the ones who tell me what is unlikely before I have to ask. If somebody says a deal is expected to slip to next quarter, and they say it on Monday, I can plan around it. If I discover it on the last day of the month, it is too late, and the problem is no longer the deal. It is the person. The other thing I value is honesty about the worst case. I do not need everybody to be optimistic. I need somebody to tell me that the run rate has leveled off, that the pipeline for next month looks thin, and what they are going to do about it. That is the report I read twice.
